nuance.usage_note: In American technical talk, classification almost always means a supervised machine learning task, as in 'a classification model' or 'a classification problem'. In government, classification means a secrecy level, as in 'the classification of the report'. In everyday speech, 'sorting' or 'categorizing' is more casual.

distinctions.note: Classification learns from labeled examples, while clustering groups unlabeled data by similarity without predefined labels.
Regression predicts a continuous number such as a price, whereas classification predicts a discrete category.
Categorization is a broader term used in psychology and everyday speech; classification is the standard term in machine learning.

examples.everyday: The photo app is pretty good at classification, so all my pictures of dogs end up in one album.
examples.professional: Our churn model is a binary classification problem, so the output is either will churn or will stay.
examples.analytical: The classification of knowledge into kinds, as Aristotle attempted, reveals assumptions about what is essential.

nuance.analogy: Like a mail sorter who puts each letter into one labeled bin, based on what they learned from past letters.
nuance.etymology: From Latin classificare, from classis ('class') and facere ('to make').
common_mistakes: Using classification as a verb; the verb is classify.
Saying 'classification predicts' when you mean the trained model; the model is the classifier, and classification is the task.

conversation.text: Classification predicts a discrete category, like spam or not spam.
We frame churn prediction as binary classification with a thirty-day window.
The report's security classification means only staff with clearance can read it.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the cloaca.

core.definition: Relating to the cloaca, the single internal chamber where the digestive, urinary and reproductive tracts meet in birds, reptiles and some other animals.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the middle syllable, -AY-, not on the first syllable. Many learners say KLOH-ay-kuhl, so make the middle syllable strong and the last syllable weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. It has no emotional charge in biology or medicine.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cloacal almost only in biology, zoology, veterinary medicine, and medicine. Ordinary speakers say 'the bird's vent' or simply 'the back end' in casual talk. In human medicine, the term appears in phrases like cloacal malformation, so the word is more likely to come up in a clinic than in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Anal refers only to the anus, while cloacal refers to a shared chamber that serves several body systems.
Rectal refers only to the rectum, so it does not cover the shared chamber found in birds and reptiles.

examples.everyday: The vet said the bird's cloacal area looked inflamed, so we're going back on Tuesday.
examples.professional: The lab report noted that the team collected a cloacal swab from each bird before the test.
examples.analytical: Comparative anatomy treats the cloacal chamber as a shared site, which complicates any simple account of separate excretory and reproductive systems.

nuance.analogy: Like a single loading dock that receives every kind of shipment for a building, instead of separate entrances for each department.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cloaca, sewer or drain, plus the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as KLOH-ay-kuhl instead of kloh-AY-kuhl.
Using cloacal as a general word for the back end of any animal, when it refers specifically to the shared internal chamber.

senses.definition: With a rough texture; not smooth.
Composed of large particles.
senses.example: coarse sand

senses.definition: Lacking refinement, taste or delicacy.
senses.example: coarse manners

senses.definition: Of inferior quality.
senses.example: Due to the internet issue, the system generated an coarse audio file.

senses.definition: Not thin; thick.

core.definition: Rough or grainy in texture, not fine or smooth; also crude or vulgar in manner or language.

pronunciation.tip: Say one strong syllable with a clear rhotic r, and do not add a vowel after it. It sounds exactly like the word 'course', so context is the only clue in speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing materials, such as coarse sand or coarse salt. Negative when describing manners, humor, or language, where it implies a lack of refinement or taste.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coarse for physical texture all the time, for example about fabric, sand, or ground pepper. When applied to people or jokes, it is a fairly direct criticism, so say it carefully in a workplace. A softer everyday alternative is rough or crude.

distinctions.note: Rough describes surface irregularity you can feel, while coarse describes a texture made of large particles or a lack of refinement.
Crude emphasizes being unrefined or primitive in method or design, while coarse more often describes texture or vulgar manners.

examples.everyday: This burlap is way too coarse to use as a bedsheet.
examples.professional: We filter out the coarse debris first, then run the fine filter on the remaining sample.
examples.analytical: Coarse-grained analysis overlooks the local variation that the finer study reveals.

nuance.analogy: Coarse is like sandpaper compared with silk: both are fabric, but one has large irregular grains you can feel.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'course', meaning ordinary or of low quality; the exact development is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing the spelling and pronunciation with 'course', which is a different word.
Calling a person coarse in a polite setting, where it sounds like a direct insult.

coarse.etymology: Adjectival use of *course* that diverged in spelling in the 18th century.

senses.definition: Characteristic of familiar conversation, of common parlance; informal.
senses.example: You're using too many colloquial words in this cover letter: I suggest changing "I picked up loads of cool skills" to "I acquired many positive abilities"

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a conversation; conversational or chatty.
A colloquial word or phrase, colloquialism.

core.definition: Used in casual, everyday conversation rather than in formal speech or writing, such as words like 'gonna' or 'kinda.'

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LOH, and the last two syllables are weak, so say 'kwee-ul' quickly. Do not stress the final syllable or say 'col-o-QUEE-al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it can label speech as too casual for a particular setting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use colloquial to describe casual words or phrases, often when talking about language or writing. In a conversation you would more often say 'casual' or 'informal.' Calling someone's email colloquial is a mild criticism, meaning it needs a more professional tone.

distinctions.note: Informal describes a relaxed situation or style in general, while colloquial specifically refers to words and expressions used in everyday speech.
Slang is usually newer, more playful, and group-specific, while colloquial language is everyday talk that most speakers use without thinking.
Vernacular refers to the everyday language of a particular region or group, while colloquial refers to the register of casual speech.

examples.everyday: Gonna is pretty colloquial, so don't use it in your cover letter, even though everybody says it.
examples.professional: The memo sounds too colloquial for a client email, so let's tighten the language before we send it.
examples.analytical: Colloquial forms like gonna reveal how speakers compress grammar in fast, low-stakes talk.

nuance.analogy: Like wearing sweatpants: fine at home or on the couch, but out of place at a wedding.
nuance.etymology: From Latin colloquialis, from colloquium 'conversation', from colloqui 'talk together'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'COL-o-kwee-al' with the wrong rhythm.
Using colloquial to mean regional or local only, when it refers to casual register.
Misspelling it as 'colloquail' or 'colloqual'.

colloquial.etymology: 1751, from earlier term *colloquy* (“a conversation”), from Latin *colloquium* (“conference, conversation”), from *con-* (“together”) + *loquor* (“to speak”), + *-al*.

senses.definition: To act in concert with; to conspire.

core.definition: To secretly cooperate with others, usually to deceive people or break rules.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, with a long oo sound like 'food'. Don't stress the first syllable, and don't add an extra vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies secret wrongdoing or an unfair arrangement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use collude mostly in news, legal and business contexts, such as companies fixing prices or officials hiding wrongdoing. In casual talk you'd say 'they were in on it together' or 'they were teaming up behind our backs'. The word almost always carries suspicion, so avoid it for ordinary teamwork.

distinctions.note: Cooperate is neutral and open; collude always implies secret and often improper cooperation.
Conspire emphasizes planning a crime or harmful plot; collude focuses on a secret arrangement, often to cheat or defeat rules.

examples.everyday: My sister and my cousin colluded to throw me a surprise party, and I had no idea.
examples.professional: The two vendors colluded to fix their bids, which triggered an antitrust investigation.
examples.analytical: Some historians argue that the bureaucracy colluded with the regime by looking away from its abuses.

nuance.analogy: Like two poker players secretly signaling across the table to beat everyone else.
nuance.etymology: From Latin colludere, 'to play together', from com- 'with' plus ludere 'to play'.
common_mistakes: Using a noun object after collude without 'with', as in 'they colluded the prices'; the usual pattern is collude with someone to do something.
Stressing the first syllable (KOH-lood) instead of the second.

senses.definition: By the way; now that I think about it; indicates something brought to mind.
senses.example: Come to think of it, it's curious that nobody was there.

core.definition: Used when a thought, fact, or memory suddenly occurs to you while you are speaking, often reversing or adding to what you just said.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on THINK. The words 'to', 'of', and 'it' are weak, so 'of' sounds like 'uhv' and the phrase runs together as 'kum-too-THINK-uhv-it'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals a friendly, thoughtful shift in conversation and is never rude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase at the start of a sentence in casual conversation, with friends, coworkers, or family, to introduce a memory that changes the topic slightly. It sounds natural in meetings too, though it is more conversational than formal writing. A typical reply is 'Oh, good point' or 'Yeah, that makes sense.'

distinctions.note: By the way introduces a new, unrelated topic, while come to think of it introduces a related memory or correction to the current topic.
Actually often corrects or contrasts what someone said, while come to think of it suggests you have just remembered something relevant.

collocations: come to think of it, I did see him
come to think of it, that is a good idea
come to think of it, we already tried that
come to think of it, I am not sure

examples.everyday: We could just order pizza. Come to think of it, we still have leftovers from Sunday.
examples.professional: Come to think of it, the Q3 dashboard already tracks that metric, so we do not need a new report.
examples.analytical: Come to think of it, the argument assumes a premise that it never defends, which undermines its conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like finding a forgotten key in your coat pocket just as you were about to call a locksmith.
nuance.etymology: Built from the idiom 'come to' (arrive at) and 'think of it'; the phrase is common in spoken English, and its exact origin is not documented.
common_mistakes: Dropping the final 'it', which sounds incomplete; say 'come to think of it', not 'come to think of'.
Using it for a formal or planned point; it signals a sudden memory, so it fits casual or spontaneous speech best.

conversation.text: Come to think of it, I haven't seen Mike in weeks.
I don't think I locked the door, come to think of it.
Come to think of it, that place does have the best pizza around.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being connected.

core.definition: In topology, the property of a space that cannot be divided into two separate open parts; more generally, the state of being connected.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, 'NEK'. The -ed after a t is pronounced as a separate syllable 'id', and the final -ness is a reduced 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in mathematics. In everyday or social science talk, 'connectedness' is positive, suggesting closeness and belonging.
nuance.usage_note: In math and computer science, connectedness is a precise term from topology and graph theory. In everyday American speech, people usually say 'feeling connected' or 'a sense of connection' instead. In psychology and public health, 'social connectedness' is a common term.

distinctions.note: A connection is a specific link between things or people; connectedness is the general state or quality of being linked.
Continuity means an unbroken sequence over time; connectedness concerns whether the parts of a whole are linked together.

examples.everyday: Our neighborhood has a real sense of connectedness, since everyone knows each other.
examples.professional: We need to check the graph's connectedness before running the clustering algorithm.
examples.analytical: Parfit argued that personal identity may rest on psychological connectedness rather than on bodily continuity.

nuance.analogy: On a road map, connectedness means you can drive from any town to any other without leaving the roads.
nuance.etymology: Formed from connected plus -ness, from Latin connectere, 'to bind together'.
common_mistakes: Using 'connectedness' in everyday talk where 'connection' or 'feeling connected' sounds more natural.
Dropping the middle syllable and saying 'kuh-NEK-ted-ness'; after a t, the -ed is pronounced 'id'.

senses.definition: To set up; to establish; to enact.
To make up; to compose; to form.
To appoint, depute, or elect to an office; to make and empower.

core.definition: To make up or form something; to be the parts that compose it, or to officially establish something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN. The unstressed syllable -stuh- is weak, and the verb differs from constitution, which stresses -TOO-.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds precise and official, suitable for formal writing and policy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use constitute in formal writing, legal language and policy discussions, as in 'constitutes a violation.' In everyday talk they say make up, form or count as. A natural meeting question is: 'Does that constitute a conflict of interest?'

distinctions.note: Make up is the everyday phrase for forming a whole; constitute is more formal and often used for legal or abstract judgments.
Compose stresses what is put together to form something, often with a focus on the parts; constitute can also mean an official establishment.
Consist of lists parts that form a whole; constitute often describes whether something counts as a particular thing.

examples.everyday: Does burning the toast once a week really constitute a kitchen emergency?
examples.professional: Two missed sprints constitute a pattern we need to address in the retrospective.
examples.analytical: For Aquinas, the soul does not merely accompany the body; it constitutes the body as the body of a human being.

nuance.analogy: Like the threads of a fabric: together they constitute the cloth, and no single thread is the whole.
nuance.etymology: From Latin constituere, 'to set up, establish', from com- 'together' and statuere 'to set up'.
common_mistakes: Confusing constitute with constitution, which is a noun for a founding document or a person's overall health.
Using constitute for physical ingredients where make up is more natural, as in 'the ingredients that make up the salad'.
Stressing the second syllable, as in kun-STYOOT, instead of KAHN-stuh-toot.

constitute.etymology: From Middle English *constituten*, from Latin *cōnstitūtum*, neuter of *cōnstitūtus*, past participle of Latin *cōnstituō* (“to put in place; set up; establish”), from *con-* (“with”) + *statuō* (“to put up; establish”).

senses.definition: To force physically, by strong persuasion or pressuring; to compel; to oblige.
To keep within close bounds; to confine.
To reduce a result in response to limited resources.

core.definition: To limit or force someone or something to act in a certain way, or to keep something within set boundaries.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STRAYN. The first syllable is a weak schwa, so do not say 'kon.' The American r is retroflex, so curl your tongue slightly back without touching the roof of your mouth.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests limits or pressure, which can be practical or unwelcome depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use constrain in business, science, engineering, and policy, often when resources, rules, or budgets limit what is possible. In casual talk, people more often say limit, restrict, or 'tie my hands.' It is a bit formal in everyday speech, so use it when you mean limits that come from outside.

distinctions.note: Restrict is more everyday and focuses on a rule or limit placed on what is allowed. Constrain often implies a limit that comes from circumstances or resources.
Compel means to force someone to do something, and it is stronger. Constrain can mean a less direct limit on choices.

examples.everyday: Our budget really constrains what we can do this summer, so we're staying close to home.
examples.professional: The project timeline constrains us to finish the migration before the end of the quarter.
examples.analytical: Human freedom is constrained by natural laws, but it is not thereby reduced to mere mechanism.

nuance.analogy: Think of a river between two banks. The banks constrain the water, shaping where it can flow without stopping it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin constringere, to bind tightly together, from com- (together) and stringere (to draw tight).
common_mistakes: Using constrain with a preposition by mistake; the usual pattern is 'constrained by' or 'constrain someone to do something.'
Confusing constrain with constraint in a sentence; the verb is constrain, and the noun is constraint.

constrain.etymology: From Middle English *constreinen*, from Old French *constreindre*, from Latin *cōnstringō*, from *cōn* + *stringō*, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **streyg-* (“to stroke, to shear, stiff”).

senses.definition: To place something or someone in a particular context.

core.definition: To explain or place something within its background, situation, or setting so it can be understood properly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEKST, and the -ize ending is pronounced lyze, rhyming with eyes. Keep the middle syllables light, with the choo sound reduced.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contextualize in academic writing, museums, journalism, and professional presentations when they want to explain why something matters. It is more formal than explain and sounds too stiff for most casual talk. A natural everyday alternative is to give some background.

distinctions.note: Explain tells what something means, while contextualize places it in a wider setting so its meaning or importance becomes clear.
Interpret focuses on finding meaning, while contextualize focuses on the background that shapes that meaning.

examples.everyday: Before you judge his comment, you should contextualize it, because he was joking about his own mistake.
examples.professional: When you present the churn numbers, contextualize them with last year's pricing change so leadership understands the trend.
examples.analytical: A careful historian must contextualize the document within the political culture that produced it.

nuance.analogy: To contextualize something is like putting a photo in its frame: the frame shows where it belongs and how to see it.
nuance.etymology: From context, from Latin contextus, with the verb ending -ize from Greek.
common_mistakes: Saying kun-TEKST-choo-uh-LYZE with stress on the last syllable.
Using contextualize as a synonym for contextual, which is an adjective.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or enforced by a contract.
senses.example: contractual rights, contractual obligations

senses.definition: A contractualized employee; One who is hired as a temporary worker, especially one who is hired for a single project.
A charge for a service that is applied through a contract with another provider.
A contract specifying details of the relationship with another country or body.

core.definition: Of, relating to, or enforced by a contract; required or defined by the terms of a written agreement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, TRAK, so the first syllable is reduced to kuhn. Do not add an extra syllable between the k and ch sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal. It signals that something is a binding obligation under an agreement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contractual in business, legal, sports, and workplace settings, such as 'a contractual obligation' or 'contractual terms'. In casual talk people usually say 'it's in the contract' or 'we're obligated to.' Using contractual in everyday conversation can sound stiff, but it is natural in emails and meetings.

distinctions.note: Contractual refers to what a contract requires, while 'legal' is broader and covers any obligation under law.
Contractible means capable of shrinking or being drawn together, so it has nothing to do with agreements.

examples.everyday: I can't cancel the gym membership early because it's a contractual commitment for a year.
examples.professional: Legal says the vendor's delivery delay is a breach of our contractual terms, so we can renegotiate the price.
examples.analytical: The distinction between contractual and fiduciary duties matters because the two carry different remedies in court.

nuance.analogy: A contractual obligation is like a promise written in ink: both sides can point to it and hold each other to it.
nuance.etymology: From contract, from Latin contractus, 'drawn together, bargain'.
common_mistakes: Confusing contractual with contractible, which is about shrinking, not agreements.
Using it for informal promises; say 'an agreement' or 'a promise' when no contract exists.

senses.definition: The state of being contrary.

core.definition: The quality of being stubbornly opposed to others, or of acting in the opposite way from what is expected or wanted.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN. Unlike contrary (adjective), the stress does not shift to the second syllable here, and the final 'ness' is a light, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes stubbornness or perversity and is rarely used as a compliment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use contrariness in casual conversation. They would more often say 'stubbornness' or 'being difficult' in everyday speech. The word appears in literature, essays, and formal descriptions of a person's temperament, such as a child who refuses everything. It is more natural to say 'his contrariness' than to build a sentence around the bare noun.

distinctions.note: Stubbornness is refusal to change one's mind; contrariness is more about deliberately doing the opposite of what is asked or expected.
Contrariety is the state of being opposed or conflicting in nature, as between two ideas; contrariness is about a person's disposition.

examples.everyday: My daughter's contrariness came out again today, and she refused to wear the jacket just because I asked her to.
examples.professional: Her contrariness in the design review slowed the project, even when her objections were valid.
examples.analytical: Dostoevsky's underground man shows a kind of contrariness that asserts freedom by rejecting reason itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a magnet that always pushes away from whatever you bring close.
nuance.etymology: From contrary, from Latin contrarius, opposite, plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with contrary, the adjective, in sentences that need a noun.
Pronouncing the middle syllables too clearly, as KAHN-trair-ee-NESS.

senses.definition: Organized, working together, cooperating.
Physically graceful or skillful.
Having coordinate bonds.

core.definition: Organized and working together smoothly, or having movements that are controlled and well timed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OR, and the final '-ated' is pronounced as 'ay-tid' with a reduced second syllable. Many learners add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests skill, planning and good teamwork.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coordinated for well-organized efforts, such as a coordinated response to a storm, and for people who move gracefully or with control. In casual talk, describing someone as coordinated is a compliment about athletic ability. It sounds a bit formal in a casual sentence, so 'well organized' may be more natural in conversation.

distinctions.note: Organized describes good planning; coordinated adds the idea that different parts are working together at the same time.
Graceful describes elegant movement; coordinated refers to the body parts moving together with control.

examples.everyday: My brother is really coordinated; he can juggle and play guitar at the same time.
examples.professional: The team showed a coordinated response to the outage, with each group handling a clear task.
examples.analytical: A coordinated political action requires shared goals and a common structure that holds the separate groups together.

nuance.analogy: A coordinated team is like an orchestra: each section plays its own part, but they follow the same score.
nuance.etymology: Past participle used as an adjective from coordinate.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllables by stressing them; the main stress is on OR.
Confusing coordinated with coordinate, which is a verb or noun in other contexts.

senses.definition: A musical instrument of the brass family, slightly smaller than a trumpet, usually in the musical key of B-flat.
A piece of paper twisted to be used as a container.
An ice cream cone (the shell itself).
The white headdress worn by the Sisters of Charity.
A kind of organ stop.
A hollow horn-like growth.
The fifth commissioned officer in a cavalry troop, who carried the colors (equivalent to the ensign in infantry).

core.definition: A brass musical instrument similar to a trumpet but shorter and wider, often played in bands and jazz ensembles.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'NET.' The 'or' is r-colored, so do not say 'KOR-net' with the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized term for a musical instrument, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cornet mainly in music classes, marching bands, brass bands, and jazz. In most casual talk, people say 'trumpet' instead. If you mean an ice cream cone, Americans say 'cone' or 'waffle cone'; 'cornet' for an ice cream cone is mainly British.

distinctions.note: A cornet is shorter, more compact, and has a mellower tone than a trumpet, though both use similar valves and similar mouthpieces.
A flugelhorn is wider and has a darker, softer sound than a cornet, and it is usually played in jazz or brass band settings.

examples.everyday: My son started playing the cornet in fifth grade band.
examples.professional: We need a second cornet player for the summer concert, so please check the sign-up sheet.
examples.analytical: The cornet's conical bore gives it a warmer, more rounded tone than the trumpet, which is why it was prominent in nineteenth-century brass bands.

nuance.analogy: A cornet is like a trumpet wearing a slightly shorter, rounder coat, with a warmer voice.
nuance.etymology: From French cornet, a diminutive of cor, horn.
common_mistakes: Saying 'KOR-net' with the stress on the first syllable.
Using 'cornet' for an ice cream cone in American English, where 'cone' is the normal word.
nuance.biblical_note: The word appears in the King James translation of Daniel 3:5, 3:7, and 3:10 as a translation of the Aramaic word qarna, meaning horn. The Revised Standard Version uses 'horn' in these passages. Key passages: Daniel 3:5 lists the horn among the instruments at the golden image. Daniel 3:7 repeats the instruments when the people bow down. Daniel 3:10 includes the horn in the summons to worship.

cornet.etymology: From Middle English *cornet*, from Old French *cornet*, a diminutive of a popular reflex of Latin *cornū* (“horn”).

senses.definition: Exhibiting or relating to crapulence.

core.definition: Relating to crapulence; sick and sluggish from overindulgence in food or drink.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, so the second syllable sounds like 'yuh'. The ending is 'lent', not 'lint'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an unpleasant state of physical sickness and dullness after too much eating or drinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use crapulent in conversation. You will meet it in older novels, essays, or formal writing about drinking. For everyday speech, use 'hungover', 'stuffed', or 'sick from drinking' instead.

distinctions.note: Both mean overindulgent in eating or drinking; crapulent is more narrowly about the resulting state, while crapulous can describe the overindulgence itself.
Hungover is common everyday English; crapulent is an older, formal word for the same kind of sickness.

examples.everyday: I felt too crapulent to get out of bed after the party, so I stayed home.
examples.professional: The executive team arrived at the retreat looking crapulent and missed the first session entirely.
examples.analytical: The essayist treats the crapulent morning-after as a moral lesson about appetite and self-control.

nuance.analogy: A crapulent person is like a car with its tank overfilled: the excess makes everything sluggish and heavy.
nuance.etymology: From Latin crapulentus, from crapula, drunkenness or hangover, from Greek kraipalē.
common_mistakes: Assuming it is related to the vulgar word 'crap' because of its sound; the two words are unrelated.
Using it in casual conversation, where it sounds old-fashioned and overly formal.

senses.definition: Not limp; firm, stiff; not stale or wilted; fresh; also, effervescent, lively.
Of air, weather, etc.: cool and dry; also, of a period of time: characterized by such weather.
Senses relating to curliness.
senses.example: crisp hair

senses.definition: Synonym of crispate (“of a leaf: having curled, notched, or wavy edges”); crisped.
Senses relating to brittleness.
senses.example: The crisp snow crunched underfoot.

senses.definition: Having a consistency which is hard yet brittle, and in a condition to break with a sharp fracture; crumbly, friable, short.
senses.example: The crisp snow crunched underfoot.

senses.definition: Of action, movement, a person's manner, etc.: precise and quick; brisk.
senses.example: An expert, given a certain query, will often come up with a crisp answer: “yes” or “no”.

senses.definition: Of fabric, paper, etc.: clean and uncreased.
Of something heard or seen: clearly defined; clean, neat, sharp.
senses.example: This new television set has a very crisp image.

senses.definition: Not using fuzzy logic; based on a binary distinction between true and false.
Of wine: having a refreshing amount of acidity; having less acidity than green wine, but more than a flabby one.
Chiefly in to a crisp: a food item that has been overcooked, or a thing which has been burned, to the point of becoming charred or dried out.
Senses relating to something brittle.
senses.example: kale crisps prawn crisp

senses.definition: A type of baked dessert consisting of fruit topped with a crumbly mixture made with fat, flour, and sugar; a crumble.
Senses relating to something curled.
A curly lock of hair, especially one which is tightly curled.
A delicate fabric, possibly resembling crepe, especially used by women for veils or other head coverings in the past; also, a head covering made of this fabric.
A banknote; also, a number of banknotes collectively.
To make (something) firm yet brittle; specifically, to give (food) a crispy surface through frying, grilling, or roasting.
senses.example: to crisp bacon by frying it

senses.definition: To become firm yet brittle; specifically, of food: to form a crispy surface through frying, grilling, or roasting.
senses.example: to put celery into ice water to crisp

senses.definition: To make a sharp crackling or crunching sound.
Senses relating to brittleness.
senses.example: to crisp bacon by frying it

senses.definition: To add small amounts of color to (something); to tinge, to tint.
Senses relating to curliness.
To curl (something, such as fabric) into tight, stiff folds or waves; to crimp, to crinkle; specifically, to form (hair) into tight curls or ringlets.
To cause (a body of water) to undulate irregularly; to ripple.
To twist or wrinkle (a body part).
To become curled into tight, stiff folds or waves.
Of a body of water: to ripple, to undulate.
Of a body part: to become twisted or wrinkled.

core.definition: Firm, fresh, and slightly brittle, like a crisp apple; also cool and dry, like crisp autumn air.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the only syllable. The r is clear and the vowel is short, like the i in 'sit'. End with a clear 'sp' sound without adding an extra vowel after the p.

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'crisp' often to praise fresh food, such as crisp lettuce or apples, and to describe pleasant cool weather in fall. It also describes clean, sharp appearances, like a crisp white shirt. In food talk, 'crispy' is often used for fried or baked foods, but 'crisp' is common for fresh produce. A natural comment is 'These apples are so crisp!'

distinctions.note: 'Crisp' is used for fresh, firm things and cool weather, while 'crispy' is mainly used for cooked foods that are crunchy.
'Crunchy' describes a sound or texture when you bite or step on something, while 'crisp' describes freshness and firmness.
'Fresh' is a general word for new or recently made, while 'crisp' emphasizes firmness and crunch.

examples.everyday: The morning is so crisp that I need a jacket for my walk.
examples.professional: Please send me a crisp summary of the findings, no more than one page.
examples.analytical: The author's crisp prose makes complex theological arguments easy to follow.

nuance.analogy: Crisp is like a fresh apple that snaps when you bite it: firm, clean, and full of life.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'crisp', curled, from Latin 'crispus', curly.
common_mistakes: Using 'crisp' for fried food when 'crispy' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the final 'sp' as 'sip' with a vowel.

crisp.etymology: The adjective is derived partly from the following:

conversation.text: I love those crisp fall mornings.
The air was cool and crisp at the top of the mountain.
These apples are so crisp and sweet.

senses.definition: A standard, test, or requirement by which individual things or people may be compared and judged; a gauge.
senses.example: criterion of choice, of decision, of selection

core.definition: A standard or test used to judge, compare, or decide something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TIR, and the last syllable is a light, reduced 'un'. Learners often say 'kri-TEER-ee-on' with a long vowel; keep the 'r' strong and the final vowel weak.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It describes a standard for judging, with no positive or negative charge in itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use criterion in business, science, education, and policy, such as 'selection criteria' for a job or grant. In casual speech people more often say 'standard', 'rule', or 'what we go by'. Criterion is singular; the plural is criteria.

distinctions.note: A standard is a general level of quality or a norm; a criterion is a specific test used to make a decision.
A benchmark is a reference point for measuring performance, often numerical; a criterion is the rule that determines the judgment.
A metric is a measured quantity; a criterion is the requirement that the measurement is judged against.

examples.everyday: My landlord has one criterion for renters: they have to pay on time.
examples.professional: Before we pick a vendor, let's agree on the criteria for evaluating their proposals.
examples.analytical: A theory of justice needs a criterion that distinguishes fair outcomes from merely efficient ones.

nuance.analogy: A criterion is like a ruler: it gives you a fixed measure to check whether something fits.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kritērion, 'means of judging', from krinein, 'to judge'.
common_mistakes: Using 'criterias' as a plural; the correct plural is 'criteria'.
Stressing the first syllable, 'KRY-teer-ee-on'; the main stress is on TIR.

criterion.etymology: From New Latin *criterion*, from Ancient Greek *κριτήριον* (“a test, a means of judging”), from *κριτής* (“judge”), from *κρίνω* (“to judge”); see critic.

senses.definition: Open to debate; not fully proved or confirmed.
senses.example: Those data are debatable: no one has been able to replicate them.

senses.definition: Able to be debated; up for discussion.
senses.example: The lack of bonuses this year is not debatable.

senses.definition: A topic that is open to debate.

core.definition: Open to dispute; not clearly proven, so people can reasonably disagree.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, the root debate, but the first syllable is a reduced schwa. Many learners stress the first syllable or drop the middle t, which in American speech is a flap sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals that something is uncertain or questionable, not necessarily wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use debatable in meetings, news, and everyday talk to say a claim is uncertain, as in 'It's debatable whether the new policy works.' It is softer than false or wrong, and it often opens a polite disagreement. The phrase 'it's debatable' is a common and gentle way to disagree.

distinctions.note: Questionable suggests doubt about honesty or quality, while debatable means reasonable people can disagree.
Doubtful means you personally are unsure, while debatable describes the question itself as open to argument.

examples.everyday: Whether pineapple belongs on pizza is debatable, but I'm not going to change my mind.
examples.professional: It's debatable whether the new dashboard will save time, so let's test it with two teams first.
examples.analytical: Whether moral virtue can be taught or must be cultivated remains a debatable question in virtue ethics.

nuance.analogy: A debatable claim is like a bridge that holds weight but still needs more testing before everyone trusts it.
nuance.etymology: From debate, from Old French debatre, to fight or contend, plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (DEB-uh-tuh-buhl) instead of the second.
Using debatable to mean only a formal debate, when it describes uncertainty or open questions.

senses.definition: A falling off, decay or descent.
The act of declining a word; the act of listing the inflections of a noun, pronoun or adjective in order.
The product of that act; a list of declined forms.
senses.example: a page full of declensions

senses.definition: A way of categorizing nouns, pronouns, or adjectives according to the inflections they receive.
senses.example: In Latin, 'amicus' belongs to the second declension. Most second-declension nouns end in '-i' in the genitive singular and '-um' in the accusative singular.

core.definition: In grammar, the set of forms a noun, pronoun or adjective takes for different cases, numbers or genders.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KLEN, the second syllable. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise term used in language and classical studies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use declension mainly in Latin, Greek, German and Russian classes, and in linguistics. The verb is decline, and the parallel term for verbs is conjugation. The older sense of decay or descent is literary and rare, so do not use it in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Conjugation refers to verb forms, while declension refers to noun, pronoun and adjective forms.
Inflection is the broader category of word endings that show grammar, and declension is one type of it for nouns and adjectives.

examples.everyday: My Latin homework has me memorizing noun declensions every night.
examples.professional: Our translation team found that the software mishandles plural adjective declensions in Russian.
examples.analytical: The genitive in the second Greek declension often carries a sense of possession that English translations flatten.

nuance.analogy: A declension is like a table of a noun's costumes, showing the form it wears for each role in the sentence.
nuance.etymology: From Latin declinatio, from declinare 'to bend aside'.
common_mistakes: Using declension for verb forms, which are conjugations.
Stressing the last syllable instead of KLEN.

declension.etymology: From late Middle English *declinson*, from Middle French *declinaison* (Modern French: *déclinaison*), from Latin *dēclīnātiō*.

senses.definition: To separate or break down (something) into its components.
senses.example: Various fungi can decompose wood.

senses.definition: To rot, decay or putrefy.
senses.example: Plastics can take centuries to decompose.

core.definition: To break something down into its component parts, or to rot and decay as organic matter does.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on POHZ. The middle syllable is reduced to a short schwa, so say 'kum', not 'kom'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In technical writing it is precise; in everyday talk about food or leaves it is plain and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use decompose in two main ways: for things rotting in nature, such as leaves or a dead animal, and for breaking a complex problem or system into parts. In software, people say decompose a problem into smaller services or functions. Saying the body decomposed can sound clinical, so people might say it rotted in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Rot is everyday and often informal, while decompose is more technical or scientific.
Break down is general and informal, while decompose names a more structured separation into components.

examples.everyday: Don't leave those banana peels in the trash for too long, because they decompose and smell bad fast.
examples.professional: Let's decompose this feature into three microservices so each team can own its deployment.
examples.analytical: To decompose an argument is to show which premises carry its weight and which are merely assumed.

nuance.analogy: Decomposing a problem is like taking apart a clock to see each gear, spring and hand before you rebuild it.
nuance.etymology: From de- (apart) plus Latin componere, to put together, from com- (together) and ponere (to place).
common_mistakes: Using decompose only for living things; it also applies to problems, systems and compounds.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, as in dee-kom-POZE; keep it reduced.

senses.definition: To consider it appropriate or worthy to do or give (something), often when it is seen as beneath one's dignity; to condescend, to vouchsafe.
To consider it appropriate or worthy to accept or take (something).
To consider it appropriate or worthy to do something, often when it is seen as beneath one's dignity; to condescend, to think fit, to vouchsafe.
senses.example: He didn’t even deign to give us a nod of the head; he thought us that far beneath him.

core.definition: To think something is worthy or appropriate to do, usually in a way that suggests you consider it beneath you.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable that rhymes with rain. Do not confuse it with den or damn, and keep the vowel long and clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative or ironic. It suggests condescension or aloofness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deign mainly in formal, literary or ironic speech, often for a snobby person who will not answer a simple question. It usually appears with a negative, as in he wouldn't deign to reply. In everyday talk, people say condescend or stoop to instead.

distinctions.note: Condescend is common and focuses on a patronizing attitude, while deign is more formal and focuses on doing something one considers beneath oneself.
Consent means agreeing, while deign suggests a grudging or aloof decision to do something.

examples.everyday: My neighbor wouldn't deign to say hello when I was carrying my groceries up the stairs.
examples.professional: The vendor wouldn't deign to explain the outage, so I escalated the ticket to his manager.
examples.analytical: The critic would not deign to engage the argument, dismissing it as beneath serious consideration.

nuance.analogy: Like a king tossing a coin to a beggar without looking up at him.
nuance.etymology: From Old French deignier, from Latin dignari (to think worthy), from dignus (worthy).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like dane, as in Great Dane; the correct sound is dayn.
Using deign for ordinary willingness; it implies condescension.

deign.etymology: From Middle English *deinen*, *deynen* (“to consider suitable to one’s dignity or worth, condescend; to appear worthy; to condescend to grant, permit, vouchsafe; to regard as worthy; to consecrate, dedicate”), from Old French *daigner*, *degnier*,…

senses.definition: The quality of being delicate.
Something appealing, usually a pleasing food, especially a choice dish of a certain culture suggesting rarity and refinement.
senses.example: a Chinese delicacy

senses.definition: Fineness or elegance of construction or appearance.
Frailty of health or fitness.
Refinement in taste or discrimination.
Tact and propriety; the need for such tact.

core.definition: A rare, expensive or especially prized food, often regarded as a special treat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DEL. The middle vowels reduce to a quick uh, and the final -cy sounds like see.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests rarity, quality and pleasure, though it can sound slightly showy when used for ordinary food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use delicacy for foods that are special or regional, such as a local specialty or an imported treat. For everyday meals, dish or food is more natural. The sense of fragility (a delicacy of touch) is more literary.

distinctions.note: A dish is any prepared food, while a delicacy is a rare or prized one.
A treat is a casual reward or sweet; a delicacy implies refinement and rarity.

examples.everyday: You have to try the baklava; it's a Greek delicacy and my favorite dessert.
examples.professional: The caterer added smoked salmon, a real delicacy, to the client's reception menu.
examples.analytical: For the critic, taste is a faculty that registers the delicacy of a dish's balance of flavors.

nuance.analogy: A delicacy is like a rare vintage wine: few people get to taste it, so it feels special.
nuance.etymology: From Latin delicatus, meaning luxurious or dainty, from deliciae, delights.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllables as full vowels; they reduce to schwa.
Using delicacy for ordinary food; save it for rare or prized dishes.

delicacy.etymology: From Middle English *delicacie*, from Middle English *delicat*, from Latin *delicatus*.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by to, and sometimes by at or on: to object or be reluctant; to balk, to take exception.
senses.example: I demur to that statement.

senses.definition: To submit a demurrer (“motion by a party to a legal action for the immediate or summary judgment of the court on the question of whether, assuming the truth of the matter alleged by the opposite party, it is sufficient in law to sustain the action or defense, and hence whether the party bringing the motion is required to answer or proceed further”).
To object or take exception to (something).
An act of objecting or taking exception; a scruple; also, an exception taken or objection to something.
An act of continuing; a continuance.
An act of lingering or tarrying.
An act of remaining or staying; a residence, a stay.
A state of having doubts; a hesitation, a pause.

Synonym of demurrer (“a motion by a party to a legal action for the immediate or summary judgment of the court on the question of whether, assuming the truth of the matter alleged by the opposite party, it is sufficient in law to sustain the action or defense, and hence whether the party bringing the motion is required to answer or proceed further”).

core.definition: To hesitate or object to something, often politely, because you disagree or feel reluctant.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the only syllable, MUR. The r is strong and the vowel is the stressed 'ur' of 'her'. Do not add a second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests reluctance, sometimes with polite resistance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'demur' mostly in writing or formal speech, such as a letter, a board meeting or a news report. In casual talk they say 'hesitate,' 'push back' or 'have reservations.' The noun 'demur' appears in phrases like 'without demur', meaning without objection, which sounds formal but natural.

distinctions.note: 'Object' is direct and common; 'demur' is softer and more polite, suggesting hesitation rather than a firm protest.
'Hesitate' can mean pausing from uncertainty; 'demur' implies reluctance to agree.

examples.everyday: When my friend suggested we drive all night, I started to demur because I was already exhausted.
examples.professional: The client demurred at the new timeline, so we agreed to revisit the scope on Friday.
examples.analytical: Several scholars demur from the author's claim that the text was written in a single period.

nuance.analogy: To demur is like pulling your hand back slightly before you touch a hot stove: a small, polite pause that signals reluctance.
nuance.etymology: From Old French demeurer, 'to delay, linger', from Latin demorari, 'to linger'.
common_mistakes: Using 'demur' as a strong refusal; it is softer than 'refuse'.
Confusing 'demur' with 'demure', which is an adjective about modesty.

demur.etymology: From Middle English *demuren* (“to delay; to linger; to remain; to keep, retain”), from Anglo-Norman *demorer* and Old French *demorer*, *demourer* (“to remain, stay”), from Vulgar Latin *dēmorāre*, from Latin *dēmorārī*, the present active infinitive of…

senses.definition: To put down; to lay down; to deposit; to lay aside; to put away.
To remove (a leader) from (high) office without killing (them).
senses.example: A deposed monarch may go into exile as pretender to the lost throne, hoping to be restored in a subsequent revolution.

senses.definition: To interrogate and elicit testimony from during a deposition, typically by a lawyer.
senses.example: After we deposed the claimant we had enough evidence to avoid a trial.

senses.definition: To take or swear an oath.
To testify; to bear witness; to claim; to assert; to affirm.
To give evidence or testimony, especially in response to interrogation during a deposition.

core.definition: To remove a ruler or high official from power, especially by force or legal action, without necessarily killing them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, POHZ, and the final sound is a voiced z. Americans often say 'pose' with a clear long o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes a serious political or legal action, and can imply a fall from power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'depose' in news about coups, revolutions, or government removals, and in history and political writing. In everyday speech, they usually say 'oust', 'overthrow', or 'kick out'. In a law context, 'depose' also means questioning a witness under oath, which is a different sense.

distinctions.note: Oust is more informal and general, often used for jobs or positions; depose is more formal and usually refers to a ruler or leader.
Overthrow emphasizes violent or sudden toppling of a government; depose can happen through legal or peaceful means.

examples.everyday: People on the news are celebrating now that the dictator has been deposed.
examples.professional: The board voted to depose the chief executive after the audit uncovered fraud.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that a monarch deposed by his own nobles reveals the fragility of feudal consent.

nuance.analogy: Like taking the crown off a king's head and placing it in another's hands, without hurting the king.
nuance.etymology: From Old French deposer, from Medieval Latin deponere, 'to put down'.
common_mistakes: Using 'depose' to mean 'depose of' a person's life; it does not imply killing.
Confusing 'depose' with 'dispose' or 'disclose'.

depose.etymology: Recorded since c.1300, from Middle English, from Old French *deposer*, from *de-* (“down”) + *poser* (“to put, place”).

senses.definition: Used with “of”, to take something away from (someone) and keep it away; to deny someone something.
To degrade (a clergyman) from office.
To bereave.

core.definition: To take something away from someone so that they no longer have it or can no longer use it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, which has the diphthong /aɪ/, so the vowel is long and clear. Make the final v a voiced /v/ sound, not an f.

nuance.connotation: negative, describing the taking away of something valued
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deprive mainly with of, as in deprive someone of something. It is common in news, law, and serious conversation, but in casual talk people often say take away, keep from, or cut off. It can sound stiff in a joking context, so use it for serious losses, such as rights, sleep, or oxygen.

distinctions.note: Rob means to steal from someone, usually by force or theft, while deprive can refer to a lack caused by any circumstance, not only crime.
Deny means to refuse to give or allow something, while deprive means to take away something a person already had or normally would have.

examples.everyday: The noise from the construction next door really deprives me of sleep.
examples.professional: The outage deprived our team of access to the production database for three hours.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that a law which deprives persons of their dignity cannot be justified by appeal to public utility.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden power cut that turns off every light in a room, deprive removes something a person was relying on.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin deprivare, from de- 'away' plus privare 'to separate, bereave'.
common_mistakes: Saying deprive from instead of deprive of.
Using deprive with a thing as the object, as in deprive the car, when the usual pattern is deprive someone of something.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible does not use the English verb deprive as a fixed technical term, but it describes the idea of taking away what belongs to another. Hebrew gazal means to rob or seize unjustly, and Leviticus 19:13 forbids defrauding or robbing one's neighbor. Paul in 1 Corinthians 7:5 tells spouses not to withhold themselves from each other except by mutual agreement for a time, which shows the idea of withholding something owed. The ethical concern is that taking away what belongs to another violates justice and love.

deprive.etymology: From Middle English *depryven*, from Old French *depriver*, from Medieval Latin *dēprīvō*, from Latin *dē-* + *prīvō*.

senses.definition: An act of disrespect or impiety towards something considered sacred.

core.definition: An act of disrespect or violation toward something considered sacred, such as a holy place or object.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on -kray-, and the first syllable has light secondary stress. Pronounce the -tion ending as shun, not tee-on.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals a grave offense against something sacred, and it is strongly condemnatory in news and public debate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use desecration in formal settings such as news stories, court cases about graves or religious sites, and public statements. In everyday talk people usually say 'disrespect' or 'damage.' The word carries a heavy moral charge, so reserve it for real sacrilege.

distinctions.note: Sacrilege is the broader term for violating something sacred, and it can be a noun for the offense or the concept. Desecration names a specific act that treats a sacred place or object with contempt.
Vandalism is a legal or everyday term for willful property damage. Desecration implies that the object's sacredness is what has been violated.

collocations: the desecration of a holy site

examples.everyday: My neighbor was furious about the desecration of the old chapel down the street.
examples.professional: The report documented the desecration of several historic churches during the riots, and the city is now planning repairs.
examples.analytical: Medieval theologians often distinguished the physical damage done to a shrine from its desecration, which was the loss of the sacred meaning that made the shrine holy.

nuance.analogy: Like a stain on a flag, desecration is damage whose real harm lies in what the object represents.
nuance.etymology: From Latin desecrare (to desecrate), from de- plus sacrare (to consecrate).
common_mistakes: Confusing desecration with decoration, which sounds similar but means something very different.
Placing the stress on the wrong syllable (des-ih-kray-SHUN).

senses.definition: To spread (something) over or through as in air, water, or other matter, especially by fluid motion or passive means.
senses.example: The small window diffuses light throughout the room.

senses.definition: To be spread over or through as in air, water, or other matter, especially by fluid motion or passive means.
senses.example: Food coloring diffuses in water.

senses.definition: Everywhere or throughout everything; not focused or concentrated.
senses.example: Such a diffuse effort is unlikely to produce good results.

senses.definition: Wordy; verbose.

core.definition: To spread out widely through a space or substance, often so that it becomes less concentrated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the vowel is a 'yoo' sound, not 'oo'. The final 's' is pronounced as 'z' here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process of spreading and is not usually good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in science, news, and formal writing. In casual talk they usually say 'spread out' or 'disperse.' In a workplace, it often describes information or responsibility being spread across many people.

distinctions.note: Spread is the everyday, general word; diffuse suggests a more even, gradual, or thin distribution.
Disperse means scattering in different directions, while diffuse often means spreading evenly through something.

examples.everyday: Let the candle burn for a minute so the smell can diffuse through the whole room.
examples.professional: We should diffuse the decision-making so that more teams can help set priorities.
examples.analytical: Foucault argues that power does not concentrate in one place but diffuses through many institutions.

nuance.analogy: Like a drop of food coloring spreading slowly through a glass of water until the whole glass has the same color.
nuance.etymology: From Latin diffundere, to pour out or spread, from dis- and fundere, to pour.
common_mistakes: Confusing the verb 'diffuse' with the adjective 'diffuse', and using the wrong form.
Pronouncing the vowel as 'dih-FOOZ' instead of 'dih-FYOOZ'.
Using 'diffuse' to mean 'confuse' or 'defuse'.

diffuse.etymology: From Middle French *diffuser*, from Latin *diffūsus*, past participle of *diffundo*, from *dis-* + *fundo*.

senses.definition: Acting in a discreet manner; acting in a way that respects privacy or secrecy; quietly.
Inconspicuously.

core.definition: In a careful, tactful way that avoids drawing attention or revealing private information.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on skreet. The final -ly is a reduced 'lee' sound, not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it implies consideration for others and good manners.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use discreetly for quietly handing something to someone, handling a problem out of sight, or checking a phone during a meeting. For example, 'She gave me a note discreetly' sounds natural. It is a positive word, though you should avoid overusing it in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Quietly describes sound level; discreetly describes care about attention and privacy, so you can speak quietly without being discreet.
Secretly means hidden on purpose, often to deceive; discreetly describes a careful, considerate way of acting.

examples.everyday: Can you discreetly let the waiter know we're ready for the check?
examples.professional: I'll raise the budget concern discreetly with Maria before the team meeting.
examples.analytical: The author discreetly withholds the verdict, letting the reader weigh the evidence for himself.

nuance.analogy: Like a stagehand moving scenery in the dark: the audience sees the play, not the work.
nuance.etymology: From discreet plus the adverbial suffix -ly; discreet is from Latin discretus, separated.
common_mistakes: Using discreetly to mean quietly in volume, as in 'speak discreetly' when you only mean softly.
Putting stress on the last syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural.

senses.definition: The state of being dissident; dissent.

core.definition: The state of openly disagreeing with an official position, party, or set of beliefs; dissent.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowels are reduced to a short uh or ih sound. Many learners say an extra syllable, so keep it to three syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive in news and political writing, where it describes principled disagreement; negative in contexts where authorities call it disloyalty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dissidence mostly in news, political analysis, and academic writing about protest or opposition movements. In everyday talk people more often say disagreement or dissent. The word is abstract, so it usually appears in the phrase 'a climate of dissidence' or as a general quality rather than about one person.

distinctions.note: Dissent is the act of disagreeing, while dissidence is the state or quality of being dissident and is more abstract and less common.
Opposition names an organized group or position against something in power, while dissidence describes the attitude or condition of dissenting.

examples.everyday: There's a lot of dissidence about the new parking rules in our building right now.
examples.professional: The team's dissidence about the migration timeline is slowing our decisions, so we need to resolve it in Thursday's meeting.
examples.analytical: Dissidence in a rigid church is not always heresy; it can be the internal pressure that forces a tradition to reexamine its foundations.

nuance.analogy: Dissidence is like a quiet crack in a dam: the state of disagreement that can grow until it changes the structure.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dissidere, 'to sit apart, disagree', from dis- 'apart' and sedere 'to sit'.
common_mistakes: Saying DIS-uh-dens with a vowel too heavy in the middle syllable instead of reducing it.
Using dissidence for a single act of disagreement; use dissent or objection for one instance.

senses.definition: In a distrustful manner.

core.definition: In a way that shows doubt or lack of trust; looking at or treating someone with suspicion.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on TRUST, the second syllable. The final '-ly' is pronounced as a short ee sound, and the middle syllables are reduced to schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a wary or suspicious manner, often in a literary or descriptive context.
nuance.usage_note: This word is rare in everyday American speech and is mostly found in fiction, journalism, and formal writing. Americans would normally say 'with suspicion,' 'warily,' or 'with doubt' in conversation. You might use it to describe how someone looked at a stranger: 'She eyed the waiter distrustfully.'

distinctions.note: 'Suspiciously' suggests you believe something is wrong, while 'distrustfully' focuses on a lack of trust in a person or thing.
'Warily' emphasizes caution and careful watching, while 'distrustfully' emphasizes doubt about trustworthiness.
'Skeptically' is more intellectual and often used for claims or evidence, while 'distrustfully' is about people or institutions.

examples.everyday: The dog watched the mail carrier distrustfully until she finally walked away.
examples.professional: The auditors reviewed the vendor's report distrustfully, since two of its figures did not match the source records.
examples.analytical: Hume's readers approached miracle reports distrustfully, weighing testimony against the regularity of nature.

nuance.analogy: Looking at something distrustfully is like checking a receipt twice before you sign it: you have not decided it is false, but you will not accept it without proof.
nuance.etymology: From 'distrustful' (dis- 'not' + trust + -ful) plus the adverb ending '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'distrustfully' in casual speech where 'suspiciously' or 'warily' is more natural.
Placing the stress on the first syllable instead of TRUST.
Forgetting the 'l' in the ending, which some learners drop.

senses.definition: Capable of being divided or split.
senses.example: Just as 12 is divisible by 3, so is 48 divisible by 12.

senses.definition: Of an integer, that, when divided by another integer, results in another integer still, thus leaving no remainder.
senses.example: Just as 12 is divisible by 3, so is 48 divisible by 12.

senses.definition: Any substance that can be divided.

core.definition: Able to be divided into parts, or, in math, able to be divided by a number with no remainder.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VIZ. The final -ible is pronounced "uh-bul," with a reduced vowel and a light "l."

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term in mathematics and a plain descriptive term in everyday use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use divisible in math classes when discussing whether a number divides evenly, and in everyday speech to say something can be split up. In casual talk, "divisible" is less common than "can be split." Be careful with spelling: the ending is -ible, not -able.

distinctions.note: Divisible is the standard spelling in both math and general use; "dividable" is a less common variant and is often marked as nonstandard.
Separable means able to be pulled apart into separate pieces; divisible often refers to splitting into equal or whole parts, especially in math.

examples.everyday: Is the pizza divisible evenly among the four of us, or should we order another one?
examples.professional: Before we write the function, we need to check whether the input values are divisible by the batch size.
examples.analytical: Whether a mathematical structure is divisible depends on how its elements combine under the given operation.

nuance.analogy: Something divisible is like a loaf of bread that can be sliced into equal pieces: some numbers slice cleanly, others leave crumbs behind.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dividere (to divide) plus -ible, meaning able to be.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "divisable" or "dividable" in formal writing.
Saying "divisible in" when you mean "divisible by" for numbers.
Stressing the first syllable as DIV-ih-zuh-bul.

divisible.etymology: From Middle English *divisible*, from Old French, from Late Latin *divisibilis*, from the verb Latin *divido*.

senses.definition: Checking that a plan or time is acceptable to all.

core.definition: A question checking whether a plan, time, or decision is acceptable to all the people involved.

pronunciation.tip: 'For' is weakened to 'fer', and 'everyone' is stressed on EV, with the middle syllable almost silent. Don't say 'ev-ree-ONE' with stress at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive and inclusive; it shows you are checking for consensus.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in meetings or group planning to confirm that a time or plan works for everyone. A natural reply is 'Yes, that works for me' or 'I think it works for everyone, but let me check with Sam.' It is friendly and not pushy, and it is common in both work and social settings.

distinctions.note: Use 'you' when speaking to one person; 'everyone' is for groups.
'Is everyone okay with that?' is more casual and emphasizes agreement, while 'Does that work for everyone?' focuses on practicality.

examples.everyday: Does that work for everyone? I'm thinking of Saturday at six for the barbecue.
examples.professional: I'm proposing a Thursday review; does that work for everyone on the team?
examples.analytical: A plan that works for everyone is not necessarily the optimal plan, but it is one the group can actually adopt.

nuance.analogy: It is like testing a bridge before everyone crosses: you want to be sure it holds for the whole group, not just the first person.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Does that work for all?' instead of 'for everyone'; 'everyone' is the natural American choice.
Pronouncing 'everyone' as 'ev-ree-one' with equal stress on all syllables.

conversation.text: Let's meet Tuesday at two. Does that work for everyone?
I'll take the slides, and Mike will handle the demo. Does that work for everyone?
Does that work for everyone, or should we find another time?
We'll launch on May 1st. Does that work for everyone?

senses.definition: The single-humped camel (Camelus dromedarius).
Any swift riding camel.

Referring to a biphasic clinical course of poliomyelitis, typically occurring in children, characterized by a minor illness, followed by an asymptomatic period of several days before the onset of a major illness involving the central nervous system.

core.definition: A one-humped camel, Camelus dromedarius, often used for riding and carrying loads in desert regions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DRAH. The middle syllable is a reduced 'muh', and the final 'ary' is a clear 'air-ee' with an audible r, not 'dree'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive word for an animal, and it sounds somewhat literary or biblical in everyday contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say camel for any camel, and use dromedary when they want to specify the one-humped kind. You will mostly hear the word in zoology, travel writing or Bible study. In casual talk you might say 'the one-humped camel'.

distinctions.note: Camel is the general term for the animal family, while dromedary specifically names the one-humped species.
A Bactrian camel has two humps and lives in Central Asia, while a dromedary has one hump and lives mainly in Africa and the Middle East.

examples.everyday: At the zoo the guide pointed to the dromedary, which has just one hump on its back.
examples.professional: Our research team tracks dromedary populations in the desert to study how they conserve water.
examples.analytical: The prophet's imagery of swift dromedaries shows how Israelite writers measured the ancient world through the animals of trade and travel.

nuance.analogy: Like a camel with a single hump, a desert workhorse with one peak.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'dromedarius', from Greek 'dromas' (runner), from 'dramein' (to run).
common_mistakes: Using dromedary for any camel; the Bactrian camel has two humps.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'dro-MED-ary'; the stress is on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The dromedary appears in Scripture as a swift riding and trade animal, and the Hebrew word usually behind camels is gamal (camel), while bikrah refers to a young female camel or swift mount. RSV Isaiah 60:6 mentions dromedaries of Midian and Ephah bringing gold and incense to Jerusalem, a picture of nations bringing wealth to God's people. RSV Jeremiah 2:23 uses the swift dromedary to describe Israel's restless wandering after other gods, showing its speed and wild movement.

dromedary.etymology: From Middle English *dromedari*, *dromedarie* (“dromedary; any camel”), from Old French *dromedaire*, from Late Latin *dromedārius* (“kind of camel”), from Latin **dromadārius*, from *dromas*, *dromadis* (“dromedary”) + *-ārius*.

senses.definition: To make or become drunk or drunken; to intoxicate.
Drunk, in the state of intoxication after having drunk an alcoholic beverage.
Given to habitual excessive use of alcohol.
Characterized by or resulting from drunkenness.
senses.example: a drunken display of crude exuberance

senses.definition: Applied to various spicy stir-fried dishes in Asian cuisine.
senses.example: drunken noodles; drunken duck; drunken fried rice

core.definition: Drunk; having had too much alcohol, or characterized by heavy drinking or drunkenness.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa, like the "en" in "ken" but very weak. Do not say a full "ayn" sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: negative; it describes intoxication in a disapproving way, often about bad behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use drunken before a noun, as in "a drunken driver" or "a drunken brawl." In everyday speech people more often say drunk. The word is also used in news and legal writing for intoxicated driving or behavior. Using drunken about a single person in a casual way can sound judgmental.

distinctions.note: Drunk is the everyday word and can be used after a verb, while drunken is more formal and usually comes before a noun.
Intoxicated is a formal, legal word, while drunken is more descriptive and emotional.

examples.everyday: The guy at the bar was getting loud and drunken, so the bartender cut him off.
examples.professional: The insurance report flagged several claims involving drunken driving last year.
examples.analytical: Paul criticizes the Corinthians who gather for the Lord's Supper and go hungry while others get drunken.

nuance.analogy: Drunken is like a sign on a road that warns of loud, unsteady behavior that others must avoid.
nuance.etymology: From drunk, with the suffix -en, from Old English druncen, the past participle of drincan, to drink.
common_mistakes: Using drunken after a verb, as in "he was drunken," where drunk is more natural.
Confusing drunken with drunkard; drunken is an adjective and drunkard is a noun.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses drunkenness as an image of spiritual confusion and as a moral warning. The Greek word methyskō means to become drunk, and it appears in Ephesians 5:18, where believers are told not to get drunk with wine but to be filled with the Spirit. In 1 Corinthians 11:21 Paul rebukes those who eat while others go hungry, and one is described as drunk. In Isaiah 29:9 the prophet describes people who are drunk, but not with wine, a figure for spiritual blindness.

drunken.etymology: From Middle English *drunken*, *ydronken*, *idrunken*, from Old English *druncen*, *ġedruncen* (“drunk; drunken”), from Proto-Germanic **drunkanaz* (“drunken”), past participle of Proto-Germanic **drinkaną* (“to drink”), equivalent to *drink* + *-en*.

senses.definition: A feeling of anger or resentment, especially haughty indignation.

core.definition: A strong feeling of offended anger or indignation, often shown in a stiff, proud way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is weak, like 'un' in 'sudden'. Do not stress the second syllable or pronounce the final part as 'gone'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes wounded pride and anger, often mocking someone for being too offended.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet 'dudgeon' in the set phrase 'in high dudgeon' or 'in a huff,' usually in writing or in playful speech. It is rarely used in everyday talk, where people say 'really upset' or 'in a huff.' Using it can sound witty or old-fashioned, depending on tone.

distinctions.note: 'Indignation' is a sober, general term for righteous anger, while 'dudgeon' often hints at the offended person being touchy or theatrical.
'Anger' is a broad, everyday word; 'dudgeon' is a more specific and often mocking word for offended pride.

examples.everyday: She stormed out of the game night in high dudgeon after someone made a joke about her cooking.
examples.professional: The vendor left the call in dudgeon when we asked for a line-item breakdown of the invoice.
examples.analytical: Their dudgeon, though sincere in tone, obscured the substance of the critique and turned the debate into a question of wounded pride.

nuance.analogy: Dudgeon is like a teakettle that has been on the stove too long: the steam is loud, and the pressure is about wounded pride.
nuance.etymology: Of uncertain origin; possibly from Scots or Welsh roots, first recorded in the 16th century. Origin is not fully settled.
common_mistakes: Using 'dudgeon' for mild annoyance; it implies strong, offended anger.
Confusing it with 'dungeon' in spelling or pronunciation.

senses.definition: Synonym of ecclesiastical.

core.definition: Relating to the Christian church as a community, especially in theology and formal writing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KLEE, the second syllable, and the middle sound is a 'zh' as in 'measure'. The 'cc' is pronounced as a 'k' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise theological term rather than an emotional word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ecclesial mainly in theology, church history and formal writing, often about the church as a living community. In everyday talk say church-related or about the church. Ecclesiastical is more common for church structures, offices and institutions.

distinctions.note: Ecclesial emphasizes the church as a community of believers; ecclesiastical emphasizes its institutions, offices and governance.
Church is the everyday word for the building, congregation or institution; ecclesial is a technical adjective.

examples.everyday: Our pastor says we are a family, not just a club, which he calls the ecclesial side of church life.
examples.professional: The seminar paper traces how the ecclesial identity of the parish changed after the reforms.
examples.analytical: Bonhoeffer argues that the Christian life is ecclesial, lived in the body of Christ rather than in private faith alone.

nuance.analogy: An ecclesial community is like a family that gathers around a shared table, not just a group of people who share a building.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin ecclesialis, from Greek ekklesia, assembly or church.
common_mistakes: Using ecclesial and ecclesiastical as perfect synonyms in every context
Stressing the first syllable instead of KLEE
